Linux is less susceptible to malware for two reasons: 1. Software is not downloaded and installed from random sites on the web. 2. User data is separate from the operating system, and programs run by the user don't have the priviledges to change the operating system. This is also true for other operating systems, but the separation is usually less absolute: The user is able to run programs with system priviledges without authentication in some cases.

It is not true that Linux is safer due to its lesser popularity: Linux is the most popular server operating system, and thus would be the most rewarding target.

It is possible to write viruses for Linux, and it has been done, but Linux viruses don't spread because of point 1 above. Even if a user account were infected, it would not affect other user accounts nor the operating system itself, and malware could easily be disabled and removed.

A rootkit in the operating system would be just as dangerous in Linux as in any other operation system. There are technologies that try to mitigate any infection, should it occur against all odds, such as AppArmor, SELinux, and stack canaries.

Linux is not invulnerable, but because of the diversity of the Linux ecosystem, exploits can only target small parts of it at a time. You should keep your system up-to-date anyway, which does not mean you need the latest release of everything, but the latest bug-fixes for your specific release from your distributor, who will provide updates not only for the operating system itself, but every application that you installed through the same system from one verified and authenticated source. Depending on your distribution, it may be able to apply them automatically without disturbing or interrupting your work.
